Abstract

1 Data valuation has garnered increasing attention in recent years, given the critical   
2 role of high-quality data in various applications. Among diverse data valuation   
3 approaches, Shapley value-based methods are predominant due to their strong   
4 theoretical grounding. However, the exact computation of Shapley values is often   
5 computationally prohibitive, prompting the development of numerous approxima  
6 tion techniques. Despite notable advancements, existing methods generally neglect   
7 the incorporation of value distribution information and fail to account for dynamic   
8 data conditions, thereby compromising their performance and application potential.   
9 In this paper, we highlight the crucial role of both global and local statistical prop  
10 erties of value distributions in the context of data valuation for machine learning.   
11 First, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of these distributions across various   
12 simulated and real-world datasets, uncovering valuable insights and key patterns.   
13 Second, we propose an enhanced data valuation method that integrates the explored   
14 distribution characteristics into the existing AME framework to refine Shapley   
15 value estimation. The proposed regularizers can also be seamlessly incorporated   
16 into various data valuation methods. Third, we introduce a novel approach for   
17 dynamic data valuation that infers updated data values without recomputing Shap  
18 ley values, thereby significantly improving computational efficiency. Extensive   
19 experiments have been conducted across a range of tasks, including Shapley value   
20 estimation, value-based data addition and removal, mislabeled data detection, and   
21 dynamic data valuation. The results showcase the consistent effectiveness and   
22 efficiency of our proposed methodologies, affirming the significant potential of   
23 global and local value distributions in data valuation.
24 1 Introduction

25 Data valuation aims to quantify the value of a datum in a dataset for various applications, including   
26 business decision-making, scientific discovery, and model training in machine learning [39, 3, 9]. It is   
27 a rapidly evolving and high-impact research topic in data-centric research communities and industrial   
28 areas, as a dataset with a large proportion of highly valuable data quite benefits real applications [10,   
29 30]. Existing data valuation methods can be broadly categorized into four groups [17]: marginal   
30 contribution-based [22, 25, 16], gradient-based [20, 18], importance weight-based [44], and out-of  
31 bag estimation-based [23] methods. Among these, the marginal contribution-based approach has   
32 emerged as the most popular and delivers strong performance. This method quantifies a datum’s value   
33 by assessing the average change in utility when the datum is removed from a set of fixed cardinality.   
34 An important index, namely, Shapley value which is a key concept in cooperative game [40, 33], is   
35 usually utilized to calculate the marginal contribution for data valuation. Due to its solid theoretical   
36 basis, Shapley value is among the primary choices in data valuation [37, 27, 22, 41]. However,   
37 the accurate calculation of the Shapley value for a given data corpus is nearly intractable as the   
38 computational complexity is about $O ( 2 ^ { N } )$ for $N$ samples. Therefore, researchers have made efforts   
39 toward the approximate yet efficient valuation methodology. For example, Jia et al. [15] investigated   
40 the scenario when data are employed for training a KNN classifier and proposed a novel efficient   
41 method, KNN Shapley, exactly in $O ( N \log N )$ time. Moreover, a recent study introduces a sparsity   
42 assumption on data values to alleviate the computational burden associated with an approximate   
43 method, specifically the Average Marginal Estimation (AME) approach [25].   
44 Although promising results are obtained, we argue that the potential of value distribution in data   
45 valuation has been largely neglected in nearly all previous studies. The sparse assumption utilized in   
46 AME actually presumes that the data values in a dataset conform to the Laplace distribution (detailed   
47 in Section 2). However, our findings indicate that this assumption may not always be justified.   
48 The value distribution in this study consists of two parts: local distribution which captures the   
49 relationship between a datum and its neighborhood, and global value distribution for all involved data.   
50 Through our empirical analysis, we have observed that the distribution of data values in a dataset   
51 more closely follows a Gaussian distribution rather than a Laplace distribution. Furthermore, our   
52 findings indicate a strong correlation among the values of nearby samples (i.e., samples within the   
53 same neighborhood). Specifically, the similarity in values between neighboring instances within the   
54 same category is pronounced, whereas the similarity between neighboring samples from different   
55 categories is minimal.   
56 Another key motivation for this study is dynamic data valuation, which involves quantifying data   
57 values in scenarios where new data is introduced or existing data is removed. To the best of our   
58 knowledge, only one existing study tries to address dynamic data valuation [46]. This pioneering work   
59 adapts the traditional Shapley value calculation into an incremental paradigm, achieving a significant   
60 reduction in computational cost—up to half—when adding or removing a datum. Building on our   
61 earlier observations where the value of an individual datum can be inferred from its surrounding   
62 neighborhood, we are inspired to explore an alternative approach to dynamic data valuation.   
63 This study investigates both the global and local distribution characteristics of data values and   
64 explores how these characteristics can be applied to both conventional and dynamic data valuation   
65 methods. First, various synthetic and real datasets are leveraged to make statistical analyses for the   
66 characteristics of global and local value distributions. Useful observations and clues are obtained on   
67 the basis of the statistical results and the discussion of previous methods. Second, two new methods   
68 for data valuation are proposed. Specifically, the first method applies the distribution characteristics   
69 to one classical Shapley value-based data valuation method, namely, AME [25]. Many existing   
70 methods can replace AME in our approach. The second method introduces a novel optimization   
71 problem that integrates distributional characteristics for dynamic data valuation, eliminating the   
72 need to re-estimate the Shapley values of the data, thus significantly improving efficiency. Third,   
73 comprehensive experiments are conducted on various benchmark datasets to evaluate the effectiveness   
74 of our methodologies in data valuation across a range of tasks.   
75 The experimental results on Shapley value estimation indicate that, compared to the AME approach,   
76 our method provides a more accurate approximation of the true Shapley values. Moreover, experi  
77 ments on value-based point addition and removal tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach   
78 in identifying both influential and poisoned samples. Furthermore, our method outperforms other   
79 data valuation techniques in mislabeled data detection tasks. Additionally, the proposed dynamic data   
80 valuation approaches consistently achieve state-of-the-art performance while significantly enhancing   
81 computational efficiency.

82 2 Related Work

Data Valuation. High-quality data play a crucial role in numerous real-world applications [7, 36, 26]. However, real-world datasets often exhibit heterogeneity and noise [24, 29]. Therefore, accurately quantifying the value of each datum within a dataset is essential for various applications and data transactions in the data market. As discussed in Section 1, existing data valuation methods can be broadly categorized into four main types:

• Marginal contribution-based methods: This kind of method calculates the differences of the utility with or without the datum to be quantified. The larger the utility difference is, the more valuable the datum is. Representative methods include leave-one-out (LOO) [17],

Data Banzhaf [38], and a series of Sharpley value-based methods such as Data Shapley [11], Beta Shapley [22], and AME [25].   
• Gradient-based methods: This kind of method evaluates the change in utility when the weight of the datum under assessment is increased. Two representative methods are Influence Function [6] and LAVA [18].   
• Importance weight-based methods: This kind of method learns an important weight for a datum to be quantified during training and takes the weight as the value [7]. Naturally, importance weight-based methods are particularly proposed for machine learning applications. One representative method is DVRL [44], which utilizes the reinforcement learning technique to learn sample weights.   
• Out-of-bag estimation-based methods: This kind of method is also designed particularly for machine learning tasks [36]. The representative method, Data-OOB [23], calculates the contribution of each data point using out-of-bag accuracy when a bagging model (e.g., random forest) is employed.

142 value distributions. To estimate the Shapley values of samples, we apply the AME method [25],   
143 setting the number of sampled subsets for each dataset to the total number of samples1. This approach   
144 ensures that the estimated scores asymptotically converge to the true Shapley values as the number of   
145 sampled subsets is large. Two statistical analyses are performed on the estimated values. The first

154 The local characteristics of value distributions are also examined across various datasets. Specifically,   
155 we investigate the relative difference between a sample and its neighbors within the same and across

162 sample’s value shows greater divergence from the values of its neighbors from different categories,   
163 with the relative difference increasing as the distance between them decreases. We have confirmed   
164 that these observations remain consistent across various datasets.

Analysis of Value Variations under Dynamic Data Conditions. Two statistical analyses are conducted to examine the variation in data values when the dataset is altered. In the first analysis, $90 \%$ of the original dataset is reserved, and the AME model is applied to compute the data values for this subset. The remaining $10 \%$ of samples are then added, and new values for all data points are recalculated. The results indicate that while the values of the original samples exhibit some variation with the addition or removal of data, these variations are relatively small. 175 Pattern Summary. Based on the aforementioned empirical analyses, the following observations   
176 and insights are summarized to guide the development of new methods:

• The distribution of data values across the entire dataset is found to more closely resemble a Gaussian distribution rather than a Laplace distribution. Therefore, in this study, the Gaussian distribution is adopted as the prior for data values. • The similarity in values between adjacent samples within the same category is substantial, while the similarity between adjacent samples from different categories is minimal. • When new data are added or existing data are removed from the original dataset, the values of samples experience changes, though these variations are relatively minor in magnitude.

4.3 Global and Local Characteristics-based Dynamic Data Valuation Approach

We further propose two dynamic data valuation methods (termed IncGLOC and DecGLOC) based on the identified global and local distribution characteristics, specifically designed for scenarios involving the addition of new data and the removal of existing data.

Here, we focus on incremental data valuation, while the optimization for decremental data valuation follows a similar approach, which is detailed in the Appendix. Let the original dataset be $\mathcal { D }$ , containing $N$ samples, and the new data to be added be $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ , with $N ^ { \prime }$ samples. The augmented dataset is denoted as $\hat { \mathcal { D } } = \mathcal { D } \cup \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ , and let $\beta ^ { c u r }$ represent the original data values in $\mathcal { D }$ .

In contrast to the only existing research on dynamic data valuation [46], which relies on recalculating Shapley values, this study investigates an alternative path that avoids the need to re-estimate Shapley values, thereby improving efficiency. Specifically, we aim to explore whether it is possible to infer the values of all data in $\hat { \mathcal { D } }$ based solely on the dataset $\hat { \mathcal { D } }$ and the original data values, $\beta ^ { c u r }$ .
As empirically analyzed in Section 3, the changes in value should align with the following insights:

• After incorporating $\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ into $\mathcal { D }$ , the values of the samples in $\mathcal { D }$ will be adjusted. However, the changes in data values before and after the inclusion of new data are anticipated to remain within a limited range.
• The global value distribution of samples in $\hat { \mathcal { D } }$ is expected to follow a Gaussian distribution.

275 4.4 Adaptation to Alternative Data Valuation Approaches

76 This study introduces a new path for data valuation that incorporates both global and local distribution   
77 characteristics of data values. The proposed regularizers can be easily integrated with most existing   
78 data valuation methods, except for the AME approach. Specifically, the regularization terms related   
79 to value distributions can be employed to optimize data values, either alongside the original valuation   
80 method or afterward. The first scenario, which combines our regularizers with other methods, has   
81 been demonstrated using the AME method. In the second scenario, the regularizers are directly   
82 utilized as optimization objectives to refine the obtained data values. This approach has also been   
83 demonstrated to enhance the effectiveness of other valuation methods, as detailed in Appendix A.7.
5 Experiments

Our experimental investigations are divided into three main components3. First, we evaluate the performance of GLOC in Shapley value estimation. Second, we examine two downstream valuation tasks: value-based point addition and removal, as well as mislabeled data detection, to validate the effectiveness of GLOC in identifying valuable and poisoned samples. 6 Conclusion

This study proposes the integration of global and local statistical information of data values into the data valuation process, a perspective that has often been overlooked by previous approaches. By examining the characteristics of value distributions, we introduce a new data valuation method based on AME that incorporates these distribution characteristics. Furthermore, we present two dynamic data valuation algorithms designed for incremental and decremental data valuation, respectively. These algorithms compute data values based solely on the original and updated datasets, alongside the original data values, without requiring additional Shapley value estimation steps, thus ensuring computational efficiency. Extensive experiments across various tasks—such as Shapley value estimation, point addition and removal, mislabeled data detection, and incremental and decremental data valuation—demonstrate the significant effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed methodologies.

• AME [25]: AME quantifies the expected marginal effect of incorporating a sample into various training subsets. When subsets are sampled from the uniform distribution, it equates to the Shapley value.   
• LOO [17]: LOO, belonging to the marginal contribution-based category, measures the utility change when one data point of interest is removed from the entire dataset.   
• Influence Function [20]: Influence Function is approximated by the difference between two average model performances: one containing a data point of interest in the training procedure and the other not.   
DVRL [44]: DVRL belongs to the importance weight-based category, involving the utilization of reinforcement learning algorithms to compute data values.   
• Data Shapley [11]: Data Shapley belongs to the marginal contribution-based category, which takes a simple average of all the marginal contributions.   
• KNN Shapley [15]: KNN Shapley is also founded on the Shapley value but distinguishes itself through the utilization of a utility tailored to $k$ -nearest neighbors.   
• Volume-based Shapley [43]: The idea of the Volume-based Shapley is to utilize the same Shapley value function as Data Shapley, but it is characterized by using the volume of input data for a utility function.   
• Beta Shapley [22]: Beta Shapley has a form of a weighted mean of the marginal contributions, which generalizes Data Shapley by relaxing the efficiency axiom in the Shapley value.   
• Data Banzhaf [38]: Data Banzhaf, also belonging to the marginal contribution-based (a) MiniBooNE (b) Electricity category, is founded on the Banzhaf value.   
• LAVA [18]: LAVA is proposed to measure how fast the optimal transport cost between a training dataset and a validation dataset changes when a training data point of interest is more weighted.   
• Data-OOB [23]: Data-OOB is a distinctive data valuation algorithm, which uses the out-ofbag estimate to describe the quality of data.

text: 616 A.7 Integration with Other Data Valuation Methods

The proposed regularization terms regarding value distributions can be seamlessly incorporated into various valuation frameworks. These regularizers can be integrated either concurrently with existing valuation methods or as a post-processing step. The first strategy, where our regularizers are applied alongside another valuation approach, has been exemplified using the AME method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these regularization terms can also function as standalone optimization objectives to refine the data values derived from other valuation techniques. Table 4 presents the performance of the original data valuation methods alongside their refined values after incorporating our proposed objectives. The results indicate that incorporating the global and local distribution characteristics of value distributions can further improve the accuracy of the data values obtained through our valuation methods, thereby enhancing detection performance.

We present additional results on value-based data point addition and removal experiments. Fig. 7 illustrates the test accuracy curves for the point removal experiment. Among the evaluated methods, GLOC generally exhibits the most significant performance degradation, suggesting its effectiveness in identifying high-quality samples. Notably, for the Electricity and MiniBooNE datasets, DVRL also performs well; however, its effectiveness is considerably lower on the other two datasets.

Fig. 8 shows the test accuracy curves for the point addition experiment. When only low-quality samples are added, GLOC demonstrates a substantial decline in performance, indicating its capability to detect and differentiate poisoned samples. These findings collectively validate the effectiveness and reliability of GLOC in data valuation.

672 A.12 Limitations

673 While the proposed global and local distribution-aided data valuation methods exhibit strong perfor  
674 mance, they also have certain limitations that present avenues for future research. First, our approach   
675 is built on the assumption that the global value distribution follows a Gaussian distribution. Although   
676 our empirical analysis across various datasets suggests that value distributions align more closely   
677 with a Gaussian distribution than with the Laplace distribution which is assumed in prior research, it   
678 is important to note that our empirical investigation can not cover all possible datasets in the world.   
679 Additionally, our study primarily focuses on global and local distributions of data values. Future   
680 research could extend our analysis by exploring value distributions across a more diverse set of   
681 datasets and considering alternative perspectives, such as hierarchical and conditional distributions of   
682 data values, to further enhance the generalizability and robustness of our approach.   
683 Moreover, although our proposed dynamic data valuation method circumvents the need for repeated   
684 Shapley value computations, its performance is inherently dependent on the quality of the existing   
685 data values. To further improve its effectiveness, one potential enhancement would be to first refine the   
686 existing data values using our proposed regularization terms before applying dynamic data valuation.   
687 This additional step could help ensure greater accuracy and robustness in the valuation process.   
688 Additionally, our current experiments cover tasks such as Shapley value estimation, value-based   
689 data addition and removal, mislabeled data detection, and dynamic data valuation. Future research   
690 is expected to explore the effectiveness of our approach in more complex data scenarios, such as   
691 cross-modal data and non-independently and identically distributed data.
